name: Kabikabi
confidence_why: Holmer 1983, the only modern first-hand description, states that stress is not significant in Kabi-Kabi or its neighbours and notes only a tendency toward the second syllable in longer words and phrases, while Mathew 1887 reports initial accent on disyllabic nouns and Goedemans 1998 files the language as second-syllable stress on Holmer's authority alone, so no fixed placement can be stated.
catalog_citation: Watson, F. J. 1944. Vocabularies of four representative tribes of south eastern Queensland, with grammatical notes thereof.. Supplement to Journal of the Royal Geographical Society of Australasia (Queensland) 48 (no. 34). Brisbane.
catalog_quote: In the vocabularies herewith, namely Kabi, Yugarabul, Wakka, and Yugumbir, the pronunciation of letters is as hereunder indicated. [...] Accent is generally on the first syllable and, to a lesser degree, on the third. There are, however, some exceptions to this rule. When the first syllable of a word ends with r the preceding vowel is sometimes obscured, and the letter r stressed so that the first and second syllables are pronounced almost as if one, as in the name of the kangaroo, i.e., kurū'man, and the native name of Mount Flinders, Burū'mpa.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 2.9 Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey. Still a certain tendency persists everywhere to stress the vowel of the second initial syllable in words or utterances of some length, as in the common Wakka-Wakka greeting wanḑá ŋin janánde where (i.e. how) are you going? Here we have two stress units, of which the former consists of two words or morphological elements; similarly in Goreng-Goreng: gilámanmin turned round, Goeng-Goeng wajálara (mountain name), goréŋ goréŋ (language name), etc. [...] Compare the common stress pattern in Aboriginal place names of the type 'Cutháraba', 'Didíllibah', 'Barálaba', all over Queensland.
new_statements.citation: Holmer, Nils M. 1983. Linguistic survey of south-eastern Queensland. Pacific Linguistics D-54. Canberra: Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: Part I 'The languages of the Wakka group', Phonetic notes, sec. 2.9, p. 5 (p. 13); cf. Kabi-Kabi sec. 21 pp. 137-138 and Batjala sec. 24 pp. 139-140 (silent on stress)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (1) Holmer 1983 PL D-54: the quoted sec. 2.9 passage is on printed p. 5 (p. 13); I verified it word for word against the saved page scan pages/diacritics wanḑá ŋin janánde, gilámanmin, wajálara, goréŋ goréŋ, Cutháraba, Didíllibah, Barálaba all as quoted; the compiler '[..]' elides one sentence on clipped forms ga < waga etc., which the report paraphrases correctly under exceptions). Scope: Part I sec. 1.1 (p. 1) lists the Wakka group as western Wakka-Wakka/Barunggam/Wuli-Wuli and eastern Goreng-Goreng/Goeng-Goeng/Kabi-Kabi/Batjala, and 2.9 says 'any of the languages dealt with in this survey.. everywhere', so the statement does cover Kabi-Kabi and Batjala, but only at group l…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Holmer (group-level, covering Kabi-Kabi and Batjala): stress is not contrastive; in words or utterances of some length the second syllable tends to carry the stress, a stress unit sometimes spanning two short words. Per the older Kabi-specific account (Mathew 1887, Curr vol. 3 p. 182): disyllabic nouns are accented 'almost invariably on the first syllable'. The two first-hand sources thus point to initial stress in disyllables (Mathew) versus a peninitial tendency in longer stretches (Holmer); no source gives a Kabi-Kabi-specific modern rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for the Wakka group; Holmer's parallel Bidjara passage (Part II p. 205, cross-referring to Part I 2.9) adds 'secondary stress appearing on subsequent alternate syllables'.
new_statements.exceptions: Holmer attributes clipped forms (Wakka-Wakka ga < waga, ḑu < ŋaḑu; Barunggam ɲaŋgu < *miɲaŋgu, ɲuŋga < waɲuŋga) to the weak first syllable; Note 14 (p. 160) rejects a claimed stress/quantity minimal pair bala· 'jewfish' vs bala 'semen' in Wakka-Wakka. Mathew 1887 limits his initial-accent claim to disyllabic substantives ('almost invariably'); his accent-marked Kabi dialogues (pp. 194ff.) show second-syllable marks on some longer words (buwan'diman, ninda'monda).
new_statements.domain_note: Holmer's tendency is explicitly about 'words or utterances of some length' and 'stress units' that may comprise two words (wanḑá ŋin), i.e. connected-speech rhythm; sec. 2.10 warns that words pronounced individually sound different from the spoken context. Mathew's statement concerns citation-form nouns.
new_statements.identity_note: Holmer 1983's stress statement (Part I sec. 2.9) is scoped to all 'languages of the Wakka group' treated in Part I (Wakka-Wakka, Barunggam, Wuli-Wuli, Goreng-Goreng, Goeng-Goeng, Kabi-Kabi, Batjala); his illustrative forms are Wakka-Wakka, Goreng-Goreng and Goeng-Goeng, none Kabi-Kabi, and he states his Kabi-Kabi data come from five rememberers and are 'quite insufficient' (sec. 20.1); Batjala (treated by Glottolog under kabi1260; Holmer's informants call it virtually the same language as Kabi-Kabi) had more informants but its phonology section (24) is likewise silent on stress. Mathew 1887 describes Kabi proper of the Mary River / Bunya Bunya country (Manumbar), i.e. kabi1260 in the narrow sense.

sources.note: Part I (Wakka group incl. Kabi-Kabi, Batjala) sec. 2.9 p. 5: stress not significant in any language of the survey; tendency everywhere to stress the second syllable in words/utterances of some length (wanḑá ŋin janánde, gilámanmin, wajálara, goréŋ goréŋ; place names Cutháraba, Barálaba). Kabi-Kabi sec. 21 (pp. 137-8) and Batjala sec. 24 (pp. 139-40): nothing on stress. Same view restated Part II 2.11 p. 178, Bidjara p. 205 (secondary stress on alternate syllables), Part III 9.6 p. 413.
